title: General and special help; Bellarmine's definition
source_text: XXVI. Rursus illud Dei auxilium internum, quo homines in agendo egent, Schola Romana distinguit in Generale & in speciale. Auxilium generale vocant, illud quo Deus cum omnibus creaturis concurrit, & in agendo iis cooperatur, sive bene, sive etiam male agant: sive ea quae faciunt sint intra naturae vires atque modum, sive naturam quadantenus superent. Nam juxta communem Scholae Romanae sensum, in ipsis malis actibus quod positivum est bonum est, nec fieri nisi Deo cooperante potest. Auxilium vero speciale dicitur, quod non datur a Deo, nisi ad actus bonos, & qui vires naturae excedunt. Ac proinde gratia auxilii specialis a Bellarmino definitur, Motio Dei qua homo ad operationes, quae naturam suam aliquo modo superant, adjuvatur.
pass_a_gloss: XXVI. Again that internal help of God, which men need in acting, the Roman School distinguishes into General and into special. They call general help, that by which God concurs with all creatures, and cooperates with them in acting, whether they act well, or even badly: whether the things which they do are within the powers and measure of nature, or surpass nature to some extent. For according to the common sense of the Roman School, in bad acts themselves what is positive is good, nor can it come to be except with God cooperating. But special help is called, that which is not given by God, except for good acts, and which exceed the powers of nature. And accordingly the grace of special help is defined by Bellarmine, The Motion of God by which man is helped to operations, which surpass his nature in some way.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXVI. The Roman School further divides this internal help of God, which men need in order to act, into general and special. General help is the help by which God concurs with all creatures and works with them in their acting, whether they act well or badly, and whether what they do lies within the powers and scope of nature or goes somewhat beyond it.

For in the common view of the Roman School whatever is positive even in evil acts is good, and cannot come about without God's cooperation. Special help is help that God gives only for good acts that exceed the powers of nature.
So Bellarmine defines the grace of special help as 'the motion of God by which man is helped toward actions that in some way surpass his nature'.
